linkages: SHARE Denmark wave 1 respondents linked to Danish administrative registers through the CPR number, which the data collection agency SFI-Survey passed to Statistics Denmark; Statistics Denmark replaced CPRs with scrambled individual identifiers
Spouses of main SHARE respondents linked through a cohabitor identification number (CNR), unique for adults sharing a street address who are married or in a registered partnership
SHARE survey measures of gross income matched to 2003 tax authority records of the same individual
SHARE survey measures of years of schooling matched to the 1970 census record (75% of the sample) or a post-1970 institutional report (25%)

sample.universe: Residents of Denmark aged 50 and above, sampled at random from the Central Person Register for the first wave of SHARE Denmark, together with their spouses
selection_rules: SHARE Denmark wave 1 interviewed 1,707 individual respondents in March 2004

Administrative records retrieved for 1,670 of the 1,707 respondents (97%); of the 37 unmatched, 21 are interviews whose main respondent appears as single in the registers and 16 (14 households) are cases where the main respondent cannot be identified
Income sample: exclude 21 outliers reporting zero income in either the survey data (19 observations) or the validation data (2 observations), leaving 1,649 observations (96.6% of the wave 1 sample)

Schooling sample: restrict to respondents born after 1920 whose education level is observed in the administrative registers; exclude nonrespondents to the SHARE education questions and the single outlier reporting zero years of schooling, leaving 1,538 observations

Robustness samples: excluding proxy interviews (1,550), excluding at least partially imputed incomes (1,088), excluding the 19 observations whose year of birth differs between survey and register (1,630), gross earnings with a nonzero reported amount (745); schooling: adding the zero-education outlier (1,539), excluding qualifications obtained abroad (1,535), excluding respondents born abroad (1,489)
sample.period: SHARE Denmark wave 1 interviews, March 2004; validation data: demographic information for January 1, 2004, tax reports for the income year 2003, and education records from the 1970 census onward

construction_notes: Gross income is the sum of the SHARE income components listed in appendix table A2 (employment, self-employment, interest from bank accounts and bonds, dividends from stocks and mutual funds, rent, long-term-care insurance, public and private pensions, unemployment and survivor benefits, life insurance, annuities, alimony and regular payments from charities); both measures are in Danish kroner in the original data and are used in logarithms

Multiple imputations of income are aggregated by respondent and their average used as if it were a nonimputed response; 35% of matched observations have at least some imputed income, on average a quarter of their income, and the unconditional proportion of imputed income is roughly 9%

Years of schooling: all three sources record the highest achieved level of education, converted to the least number of years in which that level can be obtained; data are recoded according to the SHARE conversion table (appendix table A1) except for vocational education, for which 13 years (the median imputed by Statistics Denmark) are imputed

Education registers cover 75% of the sample through the 1970 census self-report and 25% through later third-party institutional reports; qualifications obtained abroad are not recorded unless converted into an equivalent Danish degree, and the 42 immigrants in the sample are treated as self-reporting
The validation data contain the most recent education record, so differences in means between survey and validation measures are not driven by qualifications obtained after the 1970 census
Instruments for the general income model: gender and the logarithm of assets at the end of 2003, both third-party reported in the registers

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Contrary to most validation studies, we find that measurement error in income is classical once we account for imperfect validation data.
They find no evidence of mean-reverting measurement error in labor earnings (and weak evidence in pension income) for a sample of Swedish respondents.

claims.statement: In the Add Zero Outlier robustness sample, sigma_m1^2 of the general schooling measurement error model is estimated at 15.23.

treatment.label: SHARE Denmark survey self-report of years of schooling (m_s) versus the Danish administrative education register measure of the same quantity (m_r)

register_source.value: Danish official education registers (1970 census self-reports and post-1970 institutional reports)

definition.value: Not a treatment in the causal sense: the claim concerns a parameter of the measurement error model that links the two measures of the same underlying quantity. Years of schooling, obtained by converting the highest achieved level of education into the least number of years in which that level can be obtained (SHARE conversion table, appendix table A1); 13 years are imputed for all vocational education. The validation measure is the Danish education register: the 1970 census self-report for 75% of the sample and a post-1970 institutional report for 25%.

timing.value: Survey measure collected March 2004; register measure is the most recent education record

outcome.label: sigma_m1^2 (years of schooling): Variance of the true value of years of schooling in the census subsample (c = 1), i

definition.value: Variance of the true value of years of schooling in the census subsample (c = 1), i.e. among respondents whose validation data come from the 1970 census.

timing.value: Estimated on the cross-section of SHARE Denmark wave 1 respondents (survey March 2004) matched to administrative registers

units.value: squared years of schooling

estimand.target_population: SHARE Denmark wave 1 respondents born after 1920 whose education is observable in the administrative registers

population.description: SHARE Denmark wave 1 respondents born after 1920 whose education level is observable in the Danish administrative registers
population.ages: 50 and above (main respondents) and their spouses
population.period: SHARE interviews March 2004; validation data: 1970 population census and post-1970 institutional reports of qualifications
subgroups_defined: census subsample (c = 1): 75% of the sample, validation data from the 1970 census self-report
institutional-report subsample (c = 0): 25% of the sample, validation data from post-1970 third-party institutional reports
population.selection: Restricted to respondents born after 1920 for whom education level is observed in the administrative registers; nonrespondents to the SHARE education questions and the single outlier reporting zero years of schooling are excluded, leaving 1,538 observations

identification.source_of_variation: A three-way comparison of the SHARE survey report, the 1970 census self-report and post-1970 third-party institutional reports of qualifications: the sample splits into one part whose validation data are assumed error-free (institutional reports, 25%) and one whose validation data are of the same first-party nature as the survey (census, 75%), an external validation study within an internal validation study

key_assumptions.assumption: The post-1970 third-party institutional reports of qualifications (25% of the sample) are measured without error.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Qualifications are reported directly to the Ministry of Education by the institution granting them, and schooling seldom changes for seniors.

key_assumptions.assumption: The nonclassical component of measurement error is the same in the SHARE survey and in the 1970 census responses: rho_r = rho_s.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Both are first-party responses to similar questions by the same individual at different times; the model is otherwise not identified (10 exclusion restrictions, 11 parameters).

key_assumptions.assumption: The two validation subsamples (census, institutional report) need not be randomly selected; it suffices that at least one measurement error characteristic is constant across them.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The census subsample is disproportionately representative of older cohorts, with lower mean and variance of years of schooling.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on being born after 1920 and on education level being observable in the administrative registers, and excludes SHARE education nonrespondents and the single respondent reporting zero years of schooling.

implies_edges.from: born after 1920 and education level observed in the administrative registers
implies_edges.to: selection into the schooling estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Years of schooling are comparable across sources because SHARE, the 1970 census and institutional reports all record the highest achieved level of education, recoded to years with 13 years imputed for all vocational education.
No distributional assumptions on the stochastic components; identification uses first- and second-order moments only.

threats_discussed: Measurement error in bounded, ordered categorical variables such as schooling is in general negatively correlated with the true value
The 1970 census portion of the validation data is itself a first-party self-report and can be contaminated with response error
Educational qualifications obtained abroad are not recorded in the registers unless converted into a Danish degree
Vocational education cannot be mapped from Statistics Denmark levels onto SHARE levels, so 13 years are imputed
robustness_checks: Adding the single observation reporting zero years of education (appendix table A4, col. 2)
Excluding respondents stating that they received a qualification abroad (appendix table A4, col. 3)
Excluding respondents born abroad (appendix table A4, col. 4)
unresolved_confounders: The assumption rho_r = rho_s is imposed for identification and is not testable in these data
The institutional reports are assumed error-free; qualifications obtained abroad may be missing from them

estimator.value: GMM (generalized method of moments) on first- and second-order moment conditions

estimation.specification: Baseline schooling sample plus the single observation reporting zero years of education, which is excluded from the baseline for graphical presentation (appendix table A4, col. 2: Add Zero Outlier).

They find no evidence of mean-reverting measurement error in labor earnings (and weak evidence in pension income) for a sample of Swedish respondents.

claims.statement: In the No Imputations robustness sample, sigma_x^2 of the restricted income measurement error model is estimated at 0.311.

key_assumptions.assumption: The validation (register) measure is the true value: m_r = m, i.e. k_r = rho_r = sigma_r^2 = 0. The paper imposes this only as a benchmark and then relaxes it.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper presents this as the restrictive benchmark maintained by most previous validation studies, and contrasts it with the general model of cols. 2 and 4.

key_assumptions.assumption: Mismatch between survey and register records can be ignored, because SHARE Denmark drew its sample from the Central Person Register.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 97% match rate; robustness check excluding 19 observations with inconsistent year of birth.

key_assumptions.assumption: No distributional assumptions beyond finite and constant mean and variance of the error components.

threats_discussed: Unreported earnings in the validation data can produce spurious evidence of mean-reverting response error
Imputations could introduce additional nonclassical measurement error (mean reversion)
Proxy interviews are not distinguished from first-party responses in the main analysis
Mismatch of survey and register records

estimation.specification: Restricted model assuming perfect validation data, excluding incomes that have been at least partially imputed (appendix table A5, col. 3: No Imputations).

claims.statement: In the Only Earnings robustness sample, rho_s of the general income measurement error model is estimated at 0.00149 and is not significantly different from zero.

treatment.label: True value of log gross labor market earnings (m), measured in the registers as the 2003 tax authority record of earnings

register_source.value: Danish administrative tax authority records for the income year 2003 (no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper)

definition.value: Total annual gross income for 2003, the sum of all income components collected separately in SHARE wave 1 (employment, self-employment, interest, dividends, rent, pensions and other regular payments; appendix table A2), in Danish kroner, entered in logarithms; the validation measure is the corresponding 2003 Danish tax authority record.

timing.value: Income year 2003; the register measure is the 2003 tax report, the survey measure was collected in the SHARE Denmark interviews of March 2004

outcome.label: Measurement error in the SHARE survey measure of log gross labor market earnings, m_s - m

register_source.value: Constructed as the difference between the SHARE survey report and the Danish administrative register measure (2003 tax authority records)

definition.value: Additive measurement error of eq. (1): m_s = m + k_s + rho_s (m - mu_m) + eps_s. rho_s is the linear dependence between the measurement error and the true value of the quantity of interest. Total annual gross income for 2003, the sum of all income components collected separately in SHARE wave 1 (employment, self-employment, interest, dividends, rent, pensions and other regular payments; appendix table A2), in Danish kroner, entered in logarithms; the validation measure is the corresponding 2003 Danish tax authority record.

timing.value: Survey report of March 2004 against the register value for the same quantity (income year 2003)

units.value: unitless: the slope of a regression of measurement error on the true value of the quantity of interest

estimand.target_population: SHARE Denmark wave 1 respondents matched to Danish administrative registers

population.description: SHARE Denmark wave 1 respondents (a random sample of Danish residents aged 50 and above drawn from the Central Person Register, plus their spouses) matched to Danish administrative tax records for 2003
population.ages: 50 and above (main respondents) and their spouses
population.period: SHARE interviews March 2004; validation data: tax reports for the income year 2003
population.selection: SHARE Denmark drew its sample from the Central Person Register, so 1,670 of the 1,707 wave 1 respondents (97%) could be linked to administrative records; 21 outliers reporting zero income in either source are excluded, leaving 1,649 observations

identification.source_of_variation: Two independent measures of the same 2003 gross income for the same individual -- the SHARE survey self-report and the third-party-reported Danish tax register -- combined with third-party register instruments (gender and the logarithm of assets at the end of 2003) that are correlated with income but assumed independent of first-party survey response error
identification.instrument: Gender and the logarithm of assets at the end of 2003, both third-party reported in the Danish registers

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error in the Danish administrative income register is classical: it is uncorrelated with the true value of gross income (rho_r = 0).
key_assumptions.supported_by: An auxiliary regression on the random tax audit sample of Kleven et al. (2011): tax audit adjustments on postaudit gross income give a coefficient of 0.004 with a t-statistic of 0.63 (all variables in logarithms).

formal.as_written: k_r = rho_r = 0, m_r = mu_m + k_r + (m - mu_m) + eps_r (eq. [6])

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: the instruments z_m (gender and the logarithm of assets at the end of 2003) are uncorrelated with the survey measurement error eps_s except through income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The nature of third-party reporting of the instruments; Hansen's J overidentification test (p-value .606 in table 2, col. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: the instruments are correlated with the register measure of income, Cov(z_m, m_r) != 0.
key_assumptions.supported_by: First-stage F-statistic of 129.3 reported in table 2, col. 2.

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement error in the registers (third party) and in the survey are independent of each other conditional on the true value m.

key_assumptions.assumption: Mismatch between survey and register records can be ignored, because SHARE Denmark drew its sample from the Central Person Register.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 97% of respondents matched; only 19 of 1,670 matched respondents report a year of birth different from the register, and excluding them does not change the results (appendix table A5, cols. 5-6).

key_assumptions.assumption: No distributional assumptions beyond finite and constant mean and variance of the error components; identification uses first- and second-order moments only.
Multiple imputations are aggregated by respondent and used as if they were nonimputed responses, so the estimated standard errors may be biased downward.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Replication excluding all respondents subject to any form of imputation (appendix table A5, cols. 3-4).

threats_discussed: Unreported earnings in the validation data can produce spurious evidence of mean-reverting response error
Imputations could introduce additional nonclassical measurement error (mean reversion)
Proxy interviews are not distinguished from first-party responses in the main analysis
Mismatch of survey and register records
robustness_checks: Excluding proxy interviews (appendix table A5, cols. 1-2)
Excluding incomes that have been at least partially imputed (appendix table A5, cols. 3-4)
Excluding the 19 observations whose year of birth differs between survey and registers (appendix table A5, cols. 5-6)
Applying the model to gross earnings only, for respondents reporting a nonzero amount (appendix table A5, cols. 7-8)
Hansen's J overidentification test of the instruments
unresolved_confounders: The assumption that the third-party instruments have no direct influence on the first-party measurement error process except through income is untestable
Nonclassical measurement error in the validation data would change the interpretation of rho_s, which would then converge to (rho_s - rho_r)/(1 + rho_s)

estimator.value: GMM (generalized method of moments) on first- and second-order moment conditions, including an IV moment condition

estimation.specification: General model allowing classical measurement error in the validation data, applied to gross labor market earnings for respondents reporting a nonzero amount (appendix table A5, col. 8: Only Earnings).

prior_findings_compared.citation: Bound and Krueger (1991); Bound et al. (1994); Bricker and Engelhardt (2008) and most other validation studies
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Contrary to most validation studies, we find that measurement error in income is classical once we account for imperfect validation data.
They find no evidence of mean-reverting measurement error in labor earnings (and weak evidence in pension income) for a sample of Swedish respondents.
